### Bangladesh RMG Industry Data 2026 | Export Stats & Growth

[https://sdfltd.com/insights/bangladesh-rmg-industry-data/](https://sdfltd.com/insights/bangladesh-rmg-industry-data/)

Bangladesh garment export data: total RMG export value, top destination markets (EU, US, UK), knitwear vs woven split, and YoY growth.

**Q: How much does Bangladesh export in garments per year?**
A: Bangladesh's Ready-Made Garment (RMG) sector exported $39.35 billion in FY2024-25, up 8.84% from $36.15 billion the year before, according to the Export Promotion Bureau (EPB) and BGMEA.

**Q: What percentage of Bangladesh's exports come from garments?**
A: RMG exports account for over 80% of Bangladesh's total export earnings, making it by far the country's largest export sector.

**Q: Which countries buy the most garments from Bangladesh?**
A: The European Union is Bangladesh's largest RMG export market at roughly 50% of total exports, followed by the United States at around 19%, and the United Kingdom at approximately 11%, according to BGMEA/EPB data for FY2024-25.

**Q: Is Bangladesh the second largest garment exporter in the world?**
A: Yes. Bangladesh is the world's second-largest apparel exporter after China, a position it has held for over a decade.

### Custom Socks Guide | Materials & Manufacturing

[https://sdfltd.com/insights/custom-socks-guide/](https://sdfltd.com/insights/custom-socks-guide/)

Custom socks manufacturing guide. Explore bamboo and cotton materials, seamless toe options, MOQ requirements, and full production process for sock brands.

**Q: What materials are used for custom socks?**
A: Custom socks are made from various materials including combed cotton for softness and durability, bamboo fiber for moisture-wicking and sustainability, polyester for strength and shape retention, nylon for durability, and spandex for stretch and fit recovery. Material selection depends on intended use, comfort requirements, and budget considerations.

**Q: What is the sock production process?**
A: The sock production process includes yarn preparation, circular knitting on specialized machines, toe closing (seamless, hand-linked, or machine-seamed), washing and finishing, quality inspection, and packaging. Modern integrated machines can knit and close toes in one process for seamless construction. The entire process takes 2-4 weeks for custom orders.

**Q: What are seamless toe options?**
A: Seamless toe options include integrated seamless knitting where machines knit and close toes simultaneously, hand-linked toes where skilled workers close toes manually for invisible seams, and Rosso toe closing for smooth finishes. Seamless toes provide superior comfort by eliminating pressure points that can cause irritation during wear.

**Q: How do bamboo socks compare to cotton?**
A: Bamboo socks offer superior moisture-wicking, natural antimicrobial properties, and enhanced softness compared to cotton. Bamboo is more sustainable with faster growth and lower water requirements. Cotton provides excellent durability and breathability at lower cost. The choice depends on performance needs, sustainability priorities, and budget constraints.

**Q: What is the minimum order for custom socks?**
A: Custom sock minimum orders typically range from 300-500 pairs per design. Lower minimums may be available for simple designs using existing patterns. Complex custom designs with unique patterns or multiple colors require higher minimums to justify pattern development costs. Volume pricing applies with discounts for larger orders.

**Q: What customization options are available?**
A: Custom sock options include custom colors and patterns, branded labeling, custom packaging, material blends, cuff heights, and sizes. Printing options include jacquard knitting for woven patterns, sublimation for all-over printing, and embroidery for logos. Brands can create unique sock designs that align with their identity.

### Embroidery Problems Explained: Puckering & Thread Breaks

[https://sdfltd.com/insights/embroidery-problems-explained/](https://sdfltd.com/insights/embroidery-problems-explained/)

Why embroidered logos pucker or shift, what backing (stabilizer) actually does, and how stitch density limits change what's achievable on different fabrics.

**Q: Why does my embroidered logo look different on different garments?**
A: Different fabric weights and stretch levels respond differently to the same stitch file. A logo digitized and tested on woven cotton may need adjustment before it embroiders cleanly on a stretch knit.

**Q: Is puckering always a backing problem?**
A: It's the most common cause, but tension settings and stitch density also contribute. A factory experienced with your specific fabric type will usually have already solved this combination before, which is worth asking about directly.

**Q: Can a puckering problem be fixed after the garment is embroidered?**
A: Rarely, and not reliably. Puckering caused by inadequate backing is largely locked in once stitching is complete. It needs to be prevented with the correct backing choice before production, not corrected afterward.

### EU Clothing Regulations 2026 | SDF Clothing

[https://sdfltd.com/insights/eu-clothing-regulations-2026/](https://sdfltd.com/insights/eu-clothing-regulations-2026/)

Complete guide to EU clothing regulations 2026 - EPR, Ecodesign, DPP, and compliance requirements for fashion brands sourcing from Bangladesh.

**Q: Do I need to worry about the Digital Product Passport right now?**
A: Not urgently for compliance itself — textile DPP isn't legally mandatory yet, with the delegated act expected around 2027 and compliance realistically around 2028. It's worth starting to organize fiber and certification data now, since that data collection takes longer than the deadline suggests, but there's no penalty risk today.

**Q: What's the single most urgent EU regulation for a brand right now?**
A: The unsold-textile destruction ban, in effect since 19 July 2026. If your brand or your EU distributor destroys returned or surplus stock as standard practice, that needs to change now, not later.

**Q: Does sourcing from Bangladesh instead of the EU exempt me from these rules?**
A: No. EU regulations like ESPR and EPR apply based on where products are placed on the market, not where they're manufactured — a Bangladesh-made garment sold into the EU faces the same requirements as one made in Portugal.

**Q: Can my manufacturer provide the data I'll eventually need for a DPP?**
A: Ask now, before you need it. Fiber composition, chain-of-custody documentation for certified materials, and production origin records are the foundation of DPP data — a manufacturer that already tracks this for certification purposes is better positioned to support your compliance later.


---

### Fabric Cutting Explained: Bowing, Skewing, and Marker Waste

[https://sdfltd.com/insights/fabric-cutting-explained/](https://sdfltd.com/insights/fabric-cutting-explained/)

Why cut garments sometimes twist after washing, what bowing and skewing actually are, and how proper fabric relaxation and marker planning prevent both.

**Q: Is bowing and skewing more common in certain fabrics?**
A: Yes — knit fabrics, especially 100% cotton jersey, are more prone to it than wovens, because knit structures are inherently more elastic and easily distorted under tension during finishing.

**Q: Can bowing be fixed after cutting?**
A: No. Once fabric is cut with a bow or skew present, that distortion is locked into the panel shape and will show in the finished garment. It has to be addressed before cutting, through proper relaxation.

**Q: Why does marker efficiency matter to me as a buyer?**
A: Lower marker efficiency means more fabric is wasted per garment, which is typically reflected in your fabric cost. Asking about it is a reasonable, normal part of a cost discussion, especially on higher-cost fabrics.

### Fabric Types Glossary | Knit & Woven Fabric Guide

[https://sdfltd.com/insights/fabric-types-glossary/](https://sdfltd.com/insights/fabric-types-glossary/)

A-Z glossary of clothing fabric types — single jersey, interlock, pique, fleece, twill, poplin, denim and more, with GSM range and feel.

**Q: What is the difference between knit and woven fabric?**
A: Knit fabric is made by interlocking loops of yarn, which gives it natural stretch — used for t-shirts, hoodies, and activewear. Woven fabric is made by crossing two sets of yarns at right angles, which gives it structure and less stretch — used for shirts, trousers, and jackets.

**Q: Which fabric is best for t-shirts?**
A: Single jersey is the standard fabric for t-shirts, typically 140-220 GSM in 100% cotton or cotton blends. It is lightweight, breathable, and cost-effective for high-volume production.

**Q: What fabric is used for polo shirts?**
A: Pique (also spelled piqué) is the standard fabric for polo shirts. Its raised, textured knit structure holds shape better than single jersey and is typically 180-240 GSM.


---

### Fiber Blend HS Code Classification: The 50/50 Problem

[https://sdfltd.com/insights/fiber-blend-hs-classification-explained/](https://sdfltd.com/insights/fiber-blend-hs-classification-explained/)

Why a 51/49 cotton-poly blend and a 50/50 blend land in different tariff chapters, with a real CBP ruling example and Section XI Note 2.

**Q: What happens when no single fiber is more than 50% of a blend?**
A: Section XI Note 2(A) doesn't actually require 50%. A fiber only has to predominate by weight over each other single fiber individually. A 40% polyester / 35% cotton / 25% rayon fabric is classified as polyester, because 40 beats 35 and 40 beats 25, even though polyester is nowhere near a majority of the total. A genuine tie only happens when two or more fibers are exactly equal and both beat everything else — and that's rare in practice.

**Q: What actually happens in a genuine tie, like 50/50?**
A: Section XI Note 2(A) resolves it with a fixed, mechanical rule: the goods are classified under whichever heading occurs last in numerical order among the headings that equally merit consideration. This is not a judgment call about which fiber 'feels' more important — it's a numbering tie-break. A real CBP ruling (N237247) applied exactly this to a 50/50 cotton-polyester T-shirt and classified it under the man-made fiber heading, which numerically follows the cotton heading.

**Q: Does the fiber percentage on the care label determine the HS code?**
A: The care label is a starting reference, not the legal basis for classification. Customs labs measure fiber weight as oven-dry mass plus an official moisture regain allowance specific to each fiber (cotton 8.5%, polyester 0.4%), not simply 'as received' weight. If a lab result differs meaningfully from the label or invoice, the lab result overrides the paperwork.

**Q: Does a small amount of spandex or elastane change the classification?**
A: Usually not on its own. A 2-5% elastane content is normally too small to predominate over the main fibers under Section XI Note 2(A), so it typically doesn't shift the chapter by itself. But it does still count in the total fiber-weight calculation, and combined with a close cotton/polyester split it can occasionally tip a genuinely borderline blend. Report it accurately rather than rounding it out of the declared composition.

**Q: Can changing a blend ratio by a few percent really change the duty rate?**
A: Yes, and a published CBP ruling shows exactly this: a 100% cotton T-shirt (6109.10.00) carries a 16.5% duty rate, while the same style at a 50/50 cotton-polyester blend (6109.90.1090) carries 32% — nearly double, from a fabric change most people would consider a small formulation tweak.

**Q: Does recycled content (like rPET) change the HS code?**
A: No. HS classification is based on fiber type (polyester, cotton, nylon, and so on), not on whether that fiber is virgin or recycled. Recycled polyester is still classified as polyester. Recycled content can matter for other things — sustainability claims, certain trade-preference programs, or buyer requirements — but it doesn't change the tariff heading on its own.

**Q: Should I get lab testing done on blended fabric before shipping?**
A: For any blend where the split is close, yes. A third-party fiber-content lab test (ASTM D629 or ISO 1833 are the standard methods) is inexpensive relative to the cost of a customs reclassification, back-duty demand, or shipment delay, and it gives you documented evidence of composition if a customs authority later questions your declared classification.

### Garment Finishing Explained: Compacting & Softening

[https://sdfltd.com/insights/garment-finishing-explained/](https://sdfltd.com/insights/garment-finishing-explained/)

What finishing treatments do to fabric, how compacting controls shrinkage before it reaches the customer, and why handfeel matters.

**Q: Does finishing affect fabric color?**
A: It can, subtly — some finishing chemicals and heat treatments slightly shift how dyed color appears. This is one reason color approval should happen on finished fabric, not on unfinished, undyed, or unprocessed swatches.

**Q: Why does a garment feel different after the first wash than in the store?**
A: Home washing and drying continues some of the same processes finishing started — further relaxing fabric structure and softening handfeel. A well-finished garment changes only slightly after the first wash; a poorly finished one can change dramatically.

**Q: Is peach-skin finish the same as brushing?**
A: They're related but distinct processes — brushing raises fine fibers to create a soft texture, and peach-skin finish typically goes further with an additional treatment for an even softer, suede-like surface. Ask your factory specifically which one they mean when either term comes up.

### Garment Measurement (POM) Explained: Points & Tolerance

[https://sdfltd.com/insights/garment-measurement-pom-explained/](https://sdfltd.com/insights/garment-measurement-pom-explained/)

What points of measure (POM) actually are, typical tolerance ranges by measurement point, and why two garments from the same order rarely measure identical.

**Q: Who decides what tolerance is acceptable?**
A: It should be agreed between buyer and factory before production and written into the tech pack, not left to interpretation after goods are made. Most factories have a default tolerance standard, but a specific brand can request tighter tolerance on critical POMs.

**Q: Is a garment outside tolerance always rejected?**
A: Not automatically — a single POM slightly outside tolerance on a small percentage of pieces might be accepted case by case, but multiple POMs consistently outside tolerance across many pieces usually signals a real fit or grading problem worth addressing.

**Q: How many POMs should a spec sheet include?**
A: Enough to cover every dimension that matters to how the garment fits and looks — typically 10-20 points for a basic garment like a t-shirt, more for structured or multi-panel styles like jackets.


---

### Garment Washing Explained: Wash Types and Shrinkage Control

[https://sdfltd.com/insights/garment-washing-explained/](https://sdfltd.com/insights/garment-washing-explained/)

Why garments are washed as part of production, the difference between enzyme, stone, silicone, and garment-dye washes.

**Q: Does washing weaken the fabric?**
A: Some wash types, particularly stone washing, do add mechanical stress that can slightly reduce fabric strength, which is why a wash-tested pre-production sample should also be checked for strength, not just appearance.

**Q: Can garment washing fix a color mismatch from dyeing?**
A: No — washing can soften color slightly or add an intentional worn look, but it can't correct a genuine dye-lot mismatch. That has to be caught and corrected at the lab dip and bulk dyeing stage instead.

**Q: Why does the same wash recipe sometimes look different between batches?**
A: Water quality, machine load, and timing can vary slightly between wash runs, similar to how dye lots vary between dyeing runs. This is why a wash-approval swatch or reference garment should be kept and compared against each production batch.

### GOTS Label Guide | Organic Textile Certification

[https://sdfltd.com/insights/gots-label-guide/](https://sdfltd.com/insights/gots-label-guide/)

GOTS certification guide for clothing brands. Learn organic grade labeling, certification requirements, and how SDF Clothing implements textile standards.

**Q: What is GOTS certification?**
A: GOTS (Global Organic Textile Standard) is the worldwide leading textile processing standard for organic fibers. It defines environmental and social criteria for the entire textile supply chain, from organic farming to finished garments. GOTS certification ensures that products meet strict organic standards throughout production.

**Q: What are the GOTS label grades?**
A: GOTS has two primary label grades: 'organic' for products with minimum 95% certified organic fibers, and 'made with X% organic' for products with minimum 70% certified organic fibers. Both grades require that all remaining fibers meet strict ecological criteria. The organic grade represents the highest level of organic certification.

**Q: What are the labeling requirements?**
A: GOTS labeling requirements include displaying the GOTS logo, label grade, certifier name, and license number. The label must accurately reflect the organic fiber content. Only GOTS-certified products can display the GOTS logo, and certification must be maintained through annual audits. Transaction certificates verify GOTS compliance throughout the supply chain.

**Q: How does SDF implement GOTS standards?**
A: SDF Clothing implements GOTS standards through certified organic fiber sourcing, GOTS-approved chemical use in processing, social compliance in labor practices, and annual third-party audits. Our facility maintains GOTS certification with approved certification bodies, ensuring full compliance with environmental and social criteria.

**Q: What is the certification process?**
A: The GOTS certification process involves application to an approved certification body, initial audit of facilities and processes, documentation review, corrective actions if needed, and certification issuance. Annual audits maintain certification. The process typically takes 3-6 months for initial certification and requires ongoing compliance monitoring.

**Q: Why choose GOTS certified clothing?**
A: GOTS certified clothing guarantees organic fibers, no harmful chemicals, fair labor practices, and environmental sustainability throughout production. It provides consumer trust, meets regulatory requirements for organic claims, and supports sustainable fashion. GOTS is the most comprehensive organic textile certification available.

### International Size Chart Guide | US, UK, EU Size Conversion

[https://sdfltd.com/insights/international-size-chart-guide/](https://sdfltd.com/insights/international-size-chart-guide/)

Convert clothing sizes between US, UK, and EU standards for men's and women's garments, and how manufacturers build size charts.

**Q: What is a UK size 12 in US sizing?**
A: A UK size 12 in women's clothing is typically a US size 8. UK sizes generally run 4 sizes higher than US sizes for women's garments.

**Q: What is grading in clothing manufacturing?**
A: Grading is the process of scaling a base pattern (usually a middle size like Medium) up and down to create the full size range, following fixed measurement increments between each size.

**Q: How is EU size different from US size?**
A: EU sizing uses a different numbering scale entirely. A US size 8 (women's) is approximately EU size 38-40, and a US men's Medium is approximately EU size 48-50, though exact conversion varies by brand and garment type.


---

### Knitting Defects Explained: Causes and How They're Caught

[https://sdfltd.com/insights/knitting-defects-explained/](https://sdfltd.com/insights/knitting-defects-explained/)

The most common knitting fabric defects, what causes them, and how proper fabric inspection catches them before they ever reach a finished garment.

**Q: Can a knitting defect be fixed after the fact?**
A: Small, isolated defects can sometimes be avoided by cutting around them during the marker-making stage, which is exactly why fabric inspection happens before cutting. A widespread defect across a roll usually means the roll itself is rejected.

**Q: Does a cheaper yarn cause more knitting defects?**
A: Lower-quality or inconsistent yarn does increase the risk of yarn breakage and tension defects, but machine maintenance is usually the bigger factor — a well-maintained machine running mid-grade yarn often outperforms a poorly maintained machine running premium yarn.

**Q: How would I know if my order had a knitting defect problem?**
A: It typically shows up as an unusually high fabric rejection rate reported by your factory, or as a defect pattern at final inspection that repeats in the same spot across multiple garments, which points back to a specific needle or feeder issue rather than a one-off event.


---

### Lab Dip Explained: Why Color Approval Takes Multiple Rounds

[https://sdfltd.com/insights/lab-dip-explained/](https://sdfltd.com/insights/lab-dip-explained/)

What a lab dip is, why the first one is rarely approved, and what actually changes between rounds. A factory-level explanation of the color approval process.

**Q: Who pays for lab dip revisions?**
A: The first lab dip round is normally included in sampling cost. Most factories charge a small fee per additional round after the second, because each round consumes dye, lab time, and courier cost. Ask your factory to state this in writing before sampling starts, not after the third round arrives.

**Q: Can you skip the lab dip stage to save time?**
A: Only if you're using an existing, already-dyed stock fabric where the color is fixed. For any custom or Pantone-matched color on new fabric, skipping the lab dip means the bulk dye lot is your first and only chance to get the color right, with no correction possible once the fabric is dyed.

**Q: Why does the same Pantone code look different on cotton versus polyester?**
A: Pantone codes were built for ink on paper, not dye on fiber. Different fibers absorb dye differently, and a color that reads accurately on a coated paper swatch can shift several shades once it's actually dyed into cotton, polyester, or a blend. This is exactly why a physical lab dip on your actual fabric is necessary, and a digital color reference alone is not enough.

### Bangladesh Clothing Manufacturing Costs 2026 | SDF Clothing

[https://sdfltd.com/insights/manufacturing-costs/](https://sdfltd.com/insights/manufacturing-costs/)

Complete guide to clothing manufacturing costs in Bangladesh 2026 — labor rates, material prices, overhead, and total cost per garment for international brands.

**Q: Why does cost per piece drop at higher order quantities?**
A: Fixed costs — sampling, cutting setup, factory overhead per batch — get spread across more units. Fabric buying also gets more efficient at higher volumes since bulk fabric orders reduce per-kg pricing. The steepest cost drop typically happens between 300 and 1,000 pieces per style.

**Q: Are these prices FOB or landed cost?**
A: All figures are FOB Chittagong — the factory-gate price before freight, insurance, and import duty. Landed cost adds freight and duty on top, which varies significantly by destination market and product category.

**Q: Does GOTS or GRS certified fabric significantly raise the cost?**
A: Certified organic and recycled fabrics generally sit at the higher end of the material cost ranges, reflecting certification and chain-of-custody documentation costs at the mill level, but the increase is usually moderate rather than dramatic.

### Pattern & Fit Problems Explained: Grading & Tolerance

[https://sdfltd.com/insights/pattern-fit-problems-explained/](https://sdfltd.com/insights/pattern-fit-problems-explained/)

Why a perfect sample doesn't guarantee a perfect bulk fit, what grading and tolerance actually mean, and what each sample type (proto, fit, PP) is really for.

**Q: Why does the same size fit differently across two brands?**
A: Because size labels (S, M, L) aren't standardized across the industry — they're set by each brand's own size chart and block pattern. Comparing your spec sheet to your factory's block, rather than assuming a shared universal standard, is the only reliable check.

**Q: What's a reasonable number of fit-sample revision rounds?**
A: One to three rounds is typical for a new style. If it's taking more than that, the issue is usually a spec sheet that isn't precise enough at the measurement points that matter most for that garment's fit.

**Q: Should I request a PP sample even for a simple, previously-made style?**
A: Yes if it's using a new fabric lot, even on a repeat style. Fabric behavior can shift between batches enough to affect final fit, which is exactly what the PP sample stage is designed to catch before bulk cutting begins.

### Printing Methods Compared: Screen Print vs DTF

[https://sdfltd.com/insights/printing-methods-compared/](https://sdfltd.com/insights/printing-methods-compared/)

How screen printing, DTF, sublimation, and embroidery actually compare on durability and cost, and why prints crack, fade, or peel after a few washes.

**Q: Which printing method is cheapest?**
A: It depends entirely on order volume. Screen printing is cheapest per piece at high volume but has a fixed setup cost per color that makes it expensive for small runs. DTF has no per-color setup cost, making it more efficient for smaller or highly multi-colored orders.

**Q: Can I combine printing and embroidery on the same garment?**
A: Yes, and it's common for branded apparel — printing for detailed graphics, embroidery for a durable logo. Just confirm placement doesn't overlap in a way that complicates either process during production.

**Q: Why did my print look different on the actual garment than the digital mockup?**
A: Screen and monitor colors don't perfectly match physical ink or dye colors, and fabric color, texture, and absorbency all affect the final printed result. A physical pre-production sample on your actual fabric is the only reliable way to confirm a color match before bulk.

### Shade Variation Explained: Why Dye Lots Don't Always Match

[https://sdfltd.com/insights/shade-variation-explained/](https://sdfltd.com/insights/shade-variation-explained/)

Why fabric from the same order can show slightly different shades, how shade variation is measured, and what tolerance is normal versus a real quality problem.

**Q: What grey scale rating should I expect from a good factory?**
A: A rating of 4 or better is standard for most commercial orders. Rating 3 or below is generally considered a quality failure worth rejecting or renegotiating.

**Q: Can shade variation be completely eliminated?**
A: No — some lot-to-lot variation is a normal part of industrial dyeing. The realistic goal is keeping it inside an agreed, measured tolerance, not eliminating it entirely.

**Q: Does shade variation mean the factory used a cheaper dye?**
A: Not necessarily. Variation is more often caused by dyeing conditions (temperature, timing, machine load) or by mixing fabric rolls at cutting than by dye quality itself.

**Q: Should I inspect for shade variation myself or rely on the factory's QC?**
A: Both. Ask for your factory's shade-band photos as part of pre-shipment inspection, and if you use a third-party QC service, confirm shade consistency across cartons is explicitly on their checklist — it's not always included by default.


---

### Shipment Delay Explained: Why Bulk Timelines Slip

[https://sdfltd.com/insights/shipment-delay-explained/](https://sdfltd.com/insights/shipment-delay-explained/)

Why bulk production timelines differ from sample timelines, the most common real causes of delay, and how much buffer experienced buyers actually build in.

**Q: How much delay is 'normal' versus a real red flag?**
A: A few days of drift is common and usually recoverable. A delay stretching into multiple weeks without clear, specific communication about the cause is the actual red flag — a well-run factory can tell you exactly which stage is behind and why.

**Q: Does air freight fix a late shipment?**
A: It can compress the shipping leg significantly, but it doesn't fix a delay that happened during production itself, and it adds meaningful cost. It's a genuine option for the final stretch, not a substitute for keeping production on schedule from the start.

**Q: Should I ask for a production timeline before placing an order?**
A: Yes — a week-by-week timeline covering fabric, dyeing, cutting, sewing, and QC lets you see where the real risk sits in your specific order, rather than trusting a single delivery date with no visibility into how it was built.

### Stitch Quality (SPI) Explained: What Makes a Seam Strong

[https://sdfltd.com/insights/stitch-quality-spi-explained/](https://sdfltd.com/insights/stitch-quality-spi-explained/)

What stitches per inch (SPI) means, typical SPI ranges by fabric and seam type, and the most common sewing defects buyers actually encounter.

**Q: Does higher SPI always mean better quality?**
A: Not automatically. Too high an SPI on lightweight or stretch fabric can weaken the seam by over-perforating it. The right SPI is matched to the specific fabric and seam type, not simply maximized.

**Q: How is SPI actually checked on the factory floor?**
A: By counting stitches within a measured one-inch section of seam, usually with a ruler or a dedicated stitch-counting gauge, spot-checked during production rather than only at the very end.

**Q: Can a customer notice a stitch quality problem before it fails?**
A: Sometimes — visible puckering or uneven stitching is a visual warning sign. Skip stitches and marginal SPI are harder to spot without close inspection, which is exactly why factory-side quality checks matter more than relying on the finished look alone.

### Yarn Quality Explained: Yarn Count, Ring Spun vs Open End

[https://sdfltd.com/insights/yarn-quality-explained/](https://sdfltd.com/insights/yarn-quality-explained/)

What yarn count actually measures, the real difference between ring spun and open end yarn, and why yarn quality can vary even within a single order.

**Q: Does higher yarn count always mean better quality?**
A: Not automatically — it means finer yarn, which suits lightweight, smooth fabric. A heavier garment like a hoodie may intentionally use a coarser, lower-count yarn, and that's a correct choice for the product, not a lower-quality one.

**Q: How can I tell if yarn quality caused a fabric problem?**
A: Uneven fabric surface, inconsistent stretch, or unusual pilling that appears across an entire batch — rather than isolated spots — often points back to yarn consistency rather than a knitting or finishing issue.

**Q: Is recycled cotton yarn lower quality than virgin cotton yarn?**
A: Not inherently lower quality, but it does behave differently — recycled fiber is typically shorter, which can mean slightly lower yarn strength unless blended with some virgin fiber to compensate. This is a normal, manageable tradeoff for a sustainability-focused order, not a defect.
